episodes.text: At Cambridge, lived a socially dissolute undergraduate life (gambling, late nights, general high living) before his 1784-85 conversion -- a lifestyle later sources contrast pointedly with his post-conversion austerity.
Financed his own 1780 parliamentary campaign directly via inherited merchant-family wealth, winning the Hull seat at age 21 without needing a patron.

Mid-speech at a mass public political meeting (March 1784), was handed a note announcing Parliament's sudden dissolution and relayed the news to the crowd himself live from the platform; was then adopted within the hour as the Pittite candidate for Yorkshire, then the largest constituency in England, effectively unopposed.

Underwent a profound religious conversion (1784-85) that he described in his own diary as a period of acute guilt and self-reproach over how he had spent his life and privileges: "The deep guilt of my past life forced itself upon me in the strongest colours."

Seriously considered abandoning political life altogether to enter the clergy after his conversion -- a real, weighed decision -- and wrote to evangelical minister John Newton explicitly agonizing over whether to even reveal his changed convictions to anyone ("ten thousand doubts within myself... every argument against it has its foundation in pride").

Both Newton and his close political friend Pitt separately counseled him to remain in politics rather than take religious orders; he ultimately took that advice, recording afterward that his mind was "in a calm and tranquil state, more humbled."

In an October 1787 diary entry, articulated his life's dual mission explicitly ("the suppression of the Slave Trade and the Reformation of Manners") -- a single diary line multiple sources treat as the founding statement of the rest of his public career.

When his first formal Abolition of the Slave Trade bill was defeated 163 to 88 in 1791 in a political climate hostile to the cause, rather than withdrawing, publicly committed to continuing indefinitely: "Never, never will we desist till we have wiped away this scandal from the Christian name."
Continued introducing abolition bills essentially every year or two through the 1790s regardless of repeated defeat (1791, 1793, 1797, a narrow 87-83 loss in 1798, 1799).

In 1792 a watered-down "gradual abolition" compromise measure -- opposed to his own stated preference for immediate abolition -- passed instead of his original bill, a real tactical defeat and disappointment rather than a reframed win.

Began taking opium daily from age 29 on his doctor's recommendation to manage a chronic, painful bowel condition; dosage escalated over decades, his diaries record real withdrawal effects when he missed a dose and passages showing the drug's apparent effect on his mental state during difficult periods ("corrupt imaginations are perpetually rising in my mind"), and he made multiple documented attempts to quit without lasting success.

Despite this chronic illness, sustained an unusually demanding double life for years: full parliamentary and campaign work plus a four-year personal writing project that produced a bestselling book (7,500 copies in six months) mixing rational argument with openly personal religious testimony.

Lived for years (1792-97) at his cousin's Clapham house, whose library became the central meeting place of a network of about a dozen interconnected evangelical families -- sustained, cohabiting collaborative organizing over years, not merely a loose political alliance -- and was the group's acknowledged parliamentary leader.

Maintained a sustained working partnership with non-MP Thomas Clarkson showing a clear division of labor -- Clarkson traveled roughly 35,000 miles gathering firsthand evidence from sailors and slave-ship crew, feeding it to Wilberforce, who supplied the parliamentary platform Clarkson himself could not use; Clarkson publicly credited the necessity of Wilberforce's role.

After Wilberforce's death, his sons' biography was seen by Clarkson as understating his own contribution to the campaign; Clarkson responded with a public pamphlet disputing their account -- a real, documented interpersonal and legacy credit conflict within the abolitionist circle.

His life was directly threatened at points during the campaign, particularly after he publicly criticized a named slave-ship captain in Parliament; he faced physical-safety concerns, the loss of friendships, and sustained political pressure to abandon the cause, yet continued.

Was the target of sustained, personalized published criticism across his career -- accused of hypocrisy by a prominent journalist for focusing on distant slaves while ignoring British workers' conditions, denounced in pamphlets by other critics, and later accused by a planter-editor of "dreadful misrepresentations."

Deliberately maintained, by his own later account, a position as a financially-independent MP belonging to no party ("to attach himself to no party, but to be independent"), working with both Tory and Whig governments depending on the issue, and never sought or was offered cabinet office.

In 1805, even his oldest, closest political friend and by-then Prime Minister Pitt did not actively support a renewed abolition bill, which was again narrowly defeated -- evidence of real strain or divergence between the two men's political priorities even within a lasting personal friendship.

After Pitt's death and a change of government, worked with the new administration to secure a deliberately incremental partial-win measure (the 1806 Foreign Slave Trade Act, cutting off roughly three-quarters of the trade) rather than holding out only for a full all-or-nothing bill.

When the decisive 1807 abolition vote finally passed 283-16 after roughly two decades of annual or biennial defeat, the House of Commons rose and cheered him directly, and he bowed his head and wept openly at the result.

The 1807 Act abolished only the trade, not slavery itself; rather than treating the victory as complete, continued campaigning for full emancipation for the remaining 26 years of his life -- a second, even longer phase of the same core cause.

In 1824, alongside a small group of reformers, founded a second, distinct social-reform organization (the future RSPCA) late in his career, on top of the ongoing emancipation campaign -- over his life he was involved in founding, funding, or leading over sixty philanthropic and reform organizations altogether.

Progressive physical decline (chronic bowel condition, opium dependence, failing eyesight) limited his capacity for demanding parliamentary work, and he formally retired from Parliament in 1825 rather than continuing past his real capacity.

On his deathbed in July 1833, told that the Slavery Abolition Bill had finally passed Parliament, his recorded response was explicit gratitude that he had lived to witness it ("Thank God that I should have lived to witness the day..."); he died three days later.
